name: Hastings Skateboard Park
why: A big concrete park on the west side of Hastings Park, between the PNE Forum and the Italian Gardens, with three connected bowls (the deep end runs about 11 feet) and a small street area. It has hosted contests including the Vans Park Series.
heads_up: Street parking around the PNE grounds is restricted, so use PNE parking; the bowls fill up on dry summer evenings.

name: Vancouver Skate Plaza (Downtown Skateboard Plaza)
why: A 2,000 m² street plaza under the Georgia and Dunsmuir viaducts, opened in 2004 and upgraded in 2011, with replica rails, embankments, curbs, walls and steps in granite, brick, concrete and steel. Complex magazine ranked it #21 on its 2013 list of the world's best skateparks.
heads_up: The viaducts overhead keep most of it dry in the rain, but the city has long planned to remove them and replace the plaza, so check the city page before a trip.

name: Leeside Tunnel Skateboard Park
why: A volunteer-built DIY park inside an abandoned 49 m tunnel under the Cassiar Connector at East Hastings, named for skater and artist Lee Matasi, who was killed in Gastown in 2005. About a dozen hand-built mini-ramps, quarter pipes and grind poles fill the tunnel.
heads_up: Reach it down the lane behind the E-Comm building off East Pender; laneway parking is tight, so park on East Pender and keep the driveways clear.

name: China Creek Skatepark
why: Vancouver's first skatepark, opened in May 1979 on a filled-in ravine after local skaters worked with a neighbourhood committee on the design. The Vancouver Heritage Foundation named it a Place That Matters in 2022, and the Park Board has been renewing it.
heads_up: No lights, so it's a daylight session; BMX riders share the bowls, so take turns.

name: Seylynn Bowl
why: A concrete snake run that drops into a bowl, first ridden in 1978 and known as Canada's oldest surviving skatepark. Monty Little, who later designed the original Whistler park, co-designed it.
heads_up: The concrete is decades old with patches and cracks, so walk your line first; it's tucked behind trees by the ball diamonds on Hunter Street, open dawn to dusk.

name: Kensington Skateboard Park
why: A compact East Vancouver park at Knight Street and East 37th Avenue built around a pool-style bowl about 9.5 feet at the deep end and 5 feet at the shallow end, plus a mini-ramp and amphitheatre-style ledges.
heads_up: No lights; the pool bowl is deep for a small park, so newer skaters should warm up on the mini-ramp.

name: Metro Skate Park (Bonsor Park)
why: Next to Metrotown in Bonsor Park, with a street zone, a bowl zone that includes a full pipe, and a beginner section with a shallow bowl and grind curbs.
heads_up: No lights, so plan a daylight session; beginners have their own shallow-bowl section away from the full pipe.

name: Railside Skate Park
why: At the south end of Lions Park beside the rail yards, mixing a street area of rails, hips, stairs and ledges with a large bowl zone.
heads_up: It sits right beside an active rail yard, so keep clear of the tracks; there's no cover when it rains.

name: Chuck Bailey Skatepark
why: About 30,000 sq ft of concrete outside the Chuck Bailey Recreation Centre, mixing a large plaza of ramps, rails and bowls with local art, plus a 5,000 sq ft covered bowl area built for wet-weather riding.
heads_up: Only the covered bowl area stays dry in the rain; the rest of the plaza is open to the weather.

name: UBC Skatepark
why: Billed as North America's first on-campus concrete skatepark, it packs a bowled mini-ramp, ledges, rails and a ledge shaped like a stack of books into a compact spot on Thunderbird Boulevard.
heads_up: Small footprint, so watch for skaters crossing your line; there's no cover from rain.

name: Whistler Skatepark
why: Designed by Monty Little and built with Terry Snyder, it opened to skaters in August 1990 with a snake run into a 6.5 m-wide 'Snake Bowl'. Later phases driven by local skaters (the third opened in 2016) grew it past 50,000 sq ft, which the municipality counts as Canada's second-largest skatepark.
heads_up: Open April to November; the lights run until 1 a.m. on a push-button timer, helmets are recommended and mountain bikes aren't allowed. Access is through Day Lot 3.

name: Vic West Skatepark
why: Victoria's long-running park at 250 Esquimalt Road, a New Line Skateparks project first built in 2002 with a second phase in 2017, with one fully enclosed bowl, one open flow bowl and modern street terrain.
heads_up: The enclosed bowl has steel and pool coping, so wear a helmet; there's no roof, so let it dry after a shower.

name: Topaz Skatepark
why: A 3,000 m² all-wheels park built by New Line Skateparks that opened in August 2022 in Topaz Park, with a big bowl stepping from 6- and 8-foot pool-block sections to a 10-foot section with steel coping, a street line along the path and smaller beginner features.
heads_up: Floodlights switch off in sequence at 10 p.m. to signal closing; a bike pump track sits next door, so watch for riders.

name: Penticton Youthpark
why: In Riverside Park at the west end of the beach, with a very large street section of ledges, hubbas, rails, banks, quarter pipes and stair sets alongside a large flow bowl.
heads_up: It's beside a go-kart track and bumper boats, so summer days are busy; public washrooms are nearby and there's a large lot to the north.

name: One Love Indoor Skatepark
why: A non-profit indoor park that opened in October 2021 in a former grocery store in Whalley, run by the faith-based One Love International Society and led by former pro skater Dan Pageau, with wooden ramps, lessons and a skate shop.
heads_up: The wooden ramps get moved around for Sunday services, so the layout and hours change; check before you go.

name: Sidney Skatepark
why: In Tulista Park about 25 km north of downtown Victoria, pairing a bowl of varied depths with an extension and pocket with a full street section of stairs, a hubba, a handrail, a brick bank and a camel hump.
heads_up: Listed hours are 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.

name: Cowboys Park Skatepark (formerly Shaw Millennium Park)
why: Opened in 2000 on the west edge of downtown, its 75,000 sq ft of concrete is Canada's largest outdoor skatepark, with street, intermediate and advanced courses, a cloverleaf bowl and a large full pipe. Locals still call it 'Millz' after the Shaw Millennium Park name, which changed to Cowboys Park in 2024.
heads_up: The skatepark is open 24 hours, but some bowls close for the Cowboys Music Festival around Stampede (roughly mid-June to mid-July).

name: The Compound Indoor Skatepark
why: Calgary's only indoor skatepark by its own account, run by the Riders on Board snowboard club in a 20,000 sq ft warehouse with a street section, a large mini bowl, flat-ground courts and a beginner area with a 2 ft micro mini.
heads_up: A helmet and a signed waiver are mandatory, and public drop-in runs on set hours, so check the schedule first.

name: Huntington Hills Skatepark
why: One of the first three parks built in 2015 under Calgary's skatepark strategy, with a large bowl of extensions, hips, a spine and a pool-style pocket with pool coping, plus hubbas, a handrail, stairs and manual pads.
heads_up: A neighbourhood park at Centre St N and 64 Ave NW, so keep the noise down for the neighbours late in the day.

name: Southwood Skatepark
why: Another of Calgary's 2015 strategy parks, set in a quiet southwest neighbourhood park, with a flow bowl of varying depths and a radial pocket plus ledges, rails, stairs and a bank with an inset ledge.
heads_up: Listed hours are 5 a.m. to 11 p.m.; it's a residential area, so keep it respectful.

name: New Brighton Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks build in southeast Calgary whose bowl has several hips, pocket and vert extensions and a roll-in, next to a street section with two stair sets with handrails, out ledges and a long flat bar.
heads_up: Check the bowl is dry and clear of gravel before dropping in after a storm.

name: Genesis Centre Skatepark
why: Northeast Calgary's first official skatepark, built by New Line Skateparks in front of the Genesis Centre in Martindale and opened in 2019, with a large bowl and a mostly street layout of hubbas, ledges, rails and stairs.
heads_up: Listed as open 24/7; it sits in front of the Genesis Centre on Falconridge Blvd NE.

name: Castle Downs Skatepark
why: A large all-concrete park on 153 Avenue NW beside the Castle Downs YMCA, with a big flow bowl (hips, extension, roller, roll-in and a transfer spine) and a full street course.
heads_up: Open 5 a.m. to 11 p.m.; Edmonton asks skaters to ride only when the surface is dry and free of snow and ice.

name: Callingwood Skatepark
why: A 19,500 sq ft New Line Skateparks street park in west Edmonton with granite-topped hubba ledges, stair sets, handrails, gaps, manual pads and a half pipe.
heads_up: Listed hours are sunrise to sunset; it's mostly street terrain, so transition skaters may want to pair it with Castle Downs or Mill Woods.

name: Mill Woods Skatepark
why: One of Edmonton's older parks, by the Mill Woods Recreation Centre, with a bowl of hips, volcanoes and pump bumps and a brick China bank, plus ledges, rails, a Euro gap and a bank-to-bank gap.
heads_up: It's lit and open 24/7, but the older concrete has big cracks, so watch your wheels.

name: Woodlands Skatepark
why: Rebuilt on the old park's site in Legion Memorial Park in 2020, this 14,000 sq ft park has a 5–8 ft pool-style bowl, a 4 ft mini-ramp bowl, a flow bowl with a banked spine and centre island, and a street area.
heads_up: Lights stay on until 11 p.m.; the fenced park's only entrance is on the northeast side, behind the kids' water park.

name: Glendale Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks park of almost 18,000 sq ft with a pool-style bowl, a large flow bowl and street terrain of hubbas, handrails, stair sets, an A-frame ledge and a pole jam, a natural stop on the drive between Edmonton and Calgary.
heads_up: Lit and listed as open 24/7.

name: Banff Skatepark
why: A New Line Skateparks build off Sundance Road beside the town's ball diamonds, with a long snake-run bowl (hips, extensions, vert walls, pump bumps) and a street course of hubbas, stairs, handrails, a pole jam and a Euro gap.
heads_up: Open sunrise to sunset; watch for fly balls from the ball diamonds next door and give elk and other wildlife plenty of space.

name: Inland Skatepark
why: In Kin Coulee Park below Medicine Hat College, where a 13,500 sq ft addition in 2013 added an upper bowl, a hubba with two rails, and a plaza with a brick bank-to-ledge, a big three-stair, a gap and a warped 'sushi dish' manual pad.
heads_up: It's down the hill from the college on Kipling Street; the older park's terrain sits alongside the 2013 addition.

name: The Plaza at The Forks
why: Opened in 2006 at The Forks, about 44,000 sq ft of plaza with rails, ledges, banks, steps and skateable art such as the steel 'magic carpet', plus an 8,500 sq ft bowl. Designed by van der Zalm + Associates and New Line Skateparks, it was Canada's most expensive skatepark when built ($2.5 million).
heads_up: It's a busy public site, so watch for people walking through the plaza on summer evenings.

name: Píhtikwé Skatepark
why: A community-run indoor park whose name is Cree for 'come in'; it opened in Portage Place in fall 2023 and reopened in October 2026 at 323 Portage Avenue, across from Canada Life Centre, with loaner boards, lessons and family sessions.
heads_up: Drop-in sessions run Thursday to Saturday; youth $3, adults $10 and free for Indigenous skaters, and staff will help anyone who can't pay. Check the site for current times.
